text: A customer support agent built on Claude retrieves and summarizes content from user-submitted support tickets, some of which contain copy-pasted text from third-party websites. A security review finds that a ticket included hidden instructions telling Claude to email the full customer database to an external address. The agent has a tool that can send emails and a tool that can query the customer database. Which combination of controls best addresses this risk going forward?
options: Treat ticket content as untrusted input isolated from trusted instructions, and require explicit human approval or hook-based blocking before any email or database tool call triggered by that content executes
Instruct Claude in the system prompt to politely decline any requests embedded inside support ticket content
Increase the model's context window so it can better distinguish legitimate system instructions from injected ones
Disable the email tool entirely while continuing to allow unrestricted database queries on every ticket
correct_answer: Treat ticket content as untrusted input isolated from trusted instructions, and require explicit human approval or hook-based blocking before any email or database tool call triggered by that content executes
explanation: Indirect prompt injection from untrusted retrieved content is best mitigated by architectural separation of trusted instructions from untrusted data (e.g., XML delimiters), combined with enforced guardrails such as `PreToolUse` hooks, least-privilege tool scoping, or human approval gates on sensitive actions (A). A polite instruction in the system prompt (B) is not an enforceable control and can be overridden. A larger context window (C) does not address the trust boundary problem. Disabling only the email tool (D) leaves the unrestricted database query tool exposed.
section: Security and Safety - AI Application Security

text: A development team is building a Claude Agent SDK application that can execute shell commands and modify files in a customer's production repository during automated refactoring tasks. The team wants to prevent the agent from ever running destructive commands like `rm -rf` or force-pushing to the main branch, even if a crafted prompt or a compromised tool output tries to induce that behavior. Which mechanism provides the most reliable, deterministic protection against this risk?
options: Add a strongly worded warning in CLAUDE.md telling the agent never to run destructive shell commands
Rely on the model's built-in safety training to refuse harmful shell commands automatically

Implement a `PreToolUse` hook (layered with permission deny rules) that deterministically inspects and blocks matching destructive command patterns before execution, regardless of the model's reasoning
Lower the model's effort level so it performs fewer autonomous actions during refactoring
correct_answer: Implement a `PreToolUse` hook (layered with permission deny rules) that deterministically inspects and blocks matching destructive command patterns before execution, regardless of the model's reasoning
explanation: Hooks (`PreToolUse`, layered with permission deny rules and sandboxing) provide deterministic, code-level guardrails that execute outside the model's probabilistic reasoning (C), making them the reliable way to block destructive actions regardless of how the model was influenced. A CLAUDE.md warning (A) is advisory and can be bypassed by prompt injection or model error. Relying on built-in safety training (B) is non-deterministic and not guaranteed for repo-specific operations. Lowering effort level (D) affects reasoning depth and token usage, not deterministic safety enforcement.

text: A startup is integrating the Claude API into a multi-tenant SaaS product. Each tenant's backend service needs to call the Claude API on behalf of its users, and the team wants to minimize the blast radius if any single tenant's service is compromised. Which approach best reflects secure-by-design, least-privilege practice for managing API credentials in this architecture?
options: Issue one shared API key embedded in the client-side application bundle for all tenants to simplify key rotation
Issue a single organization-wide API key with full privileges and store it in each tenant service's environment variables
Hard-code the API key directly in the backend source code and rely on private repository access controls for protection
Provision separate, scoped API keys or credentials per tenant/service with the minimum permissions needed, store them in a secrets manager, and rotate and monitor them independently
correct_answer: Provision separate, scoped API keys or credentials per tenant/service with the minimum permissions needed, store them in a secrets manager, and rotate and monitor them independently
explanation: Least-privilege identity and secrets management (D) means isolating credentials per tenant/service (or workspace), storing them in a secrets manager (never in source code or client bundles), and enabling independent rotation and access monitoring so a single compromise does not expose other tenants. Embedding keys client-side (A) exposes them publicly. A single shared full-privilege key (B) maximizes blast radius. Hard-coding credentials in source code (C) is a critical security anti-pattern.
section: Security and Safety - Identity, Secrets, and Key Management

text: A healthcare application uses Claude to draft patient communication summaries from clinical notes that may contain protected health information (PHI). The compliance team requires that PHI never be sent to logging or analytics systems in plaintext, and that only authorized staff can view full unredacted model outputs. Which combination of practices best satisfies these requirements while still allowing the application to function?
options: Send full clinical notes to Claude as-is, and disable all application logging and tracing so nothing is ever recorded

Apply PII/PHI redaction or tokenization before data leaves trusted systems where feasible, encrypt data in transit and at rest, restrict output access via role-based authorization, and ensure any logs or traces mask sensitive fields
Allow any authenticated application user to view raw model outputs and traces, since authentication alone satisfies confidentiality requirements
Rely solely on Claude's safety training to avoid outputting PHI, without adding application-level controls
correct_answer: Apply PII/PHI redaction or tokenization before data leaves trusted systems where feasible, encrypt data in transit and at rest, restrict output access via role-based authorization, and ensure any logs or traces mask sensitive fields
explanation: Protecting sensitive data (B) requires layered application-level controls: minimizing exposure through redaction/tokenization, encrypting data in transit and at rest, enforcing role-based authorization (not just authentication) for least privilege, and masking sensitive fields in logs and traces to prevent leakage. Disabling all logging (A) breaks observability and auditing without addressing input/output authorization. Authentication alone (C) does not enforce role-based authorization. Relying only on model behavior (D) ignores necessary application-layer safeguards.
section: Security and Safety - AI Application Security

text: A company is deploying a Claude-powered chatbot on a public-facing website. Legal and trust & safety teams require that the bot never produce content violating the company's content policy, even under adversarial jailbreak attempts, and that failures be caught at multiple points rather than relying on a single safeguard. Which deployment strategy best reflects this requirement?
options: Layer multiple guardrails: system-level instructions, input/output content filtering or classifiers, hook-based enforcement for sensitive actions, and ongoing monitoring of production outputs
Rely exclusively on a single, carefully worded system prompt instructing the model to follow the company's content policy
Use the largest available Opus model tier, since model capability alone guarantees policy compliance under adversarial inputs
Skip guardrails at initial launch and add them reactively only if a policy violation is reported by an end user
correct_answer: Layer multiple guardrails: system-level instructions, input/output content filtering or classifiers, hook-based enforcement for sensitive actions, and ongoing monitoring of production outputs
explanation: Safe deployment practice emphasizes defense-in-depth (A): no single control (including system prompts or model capability alone) is sufficient against adversarial jailbreak attempts. Layering guardrails—prompt-level instructions, input/output classifiers and filters, deterministic hooks, and production monitoring—provides redundancy so that if one layer fails, others catch violations. Relying on a system prompt alone (B) or model size alone (C) is insufficient, and reactive-only approaches (D) expose users to harm before detection.
section: Security and Safety - Guardrails and Safe Deployment
